intro: Awadagin Pratt plays a two-minute drama for the piano: a melody in octaves, a left hand leaping across the keyboard, and a return that makes both hands carry the storm.

sections.label: A · Octaves above a leaping bass
sections.mNote: The right hand sings; the left hand crosses the keyboard

sections.label: B · The octave melody softens
sections.mNote: The melody eases while the left-hand triplets continue

sections.label: A′ · Chords crowd around the melody
sections.mNote: Both hands now play triplet chords beneath the tune

sections.label: Coda · A sweep and three chords
sections.mNote: Both hands climb before the final D♯ minor chords

relations.label: The octave melody returns
relations.basis: The A′ section intensifies the opening D♯-minor material after the quieter middle. These excerpts compare a phrase from the first section with its return inside the section marked near 64 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.930, sustained 12 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 51 s (cache/form/scriabin-etude-op8-12.txt, candidate 2; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Octaves over the left hand
cues.text: The right hand sings in octaves while the left hand leaps between bass notes and widely spaced chords. Scriabin marks the étude Patetico. The tune moves in two against the accompaniment’s three: even this great shout has a tug inside it.
cues.evidence: Scriabin, Op. 8 No. 12, bars 1–16; score typeset by Scott Gorrie (2007), pp. 2–3. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/f3/IMSLP273680-PMLP07375-Scriabin_Op.8_No_12.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The publisher has to wait
cues.text: In March 1895 Scriabin is still revising the études, with his publisher Belyayev waiting. He writes that he works from getting up until evening: “I do not want to publish anything unfinished.” The D♯ minor étude is among the pieces he has rewritten.
cues.evidence: Scriabin to Mitrofan Belyayev, March 1895, Letters, edited by Alexey Kashperov (2003), pp. 91–92; quoted in Valentina Rubcova’s preface to Henle HN 1486. Translation from the German quotation. https://www.henle.de/media/56/3c/dd/1697725817/1486-1697725817-sync.pdf

cues.title: Both hands carry the storm
cues.text: The opening tune returns in D♯ minor, with triplet chords now crowding into both hands. The right hand has two jobs: hammer out the accompaniment and keep the longer melody singing above it. Scriabin then sends both hands climbing towards the final chords.
cues.evidence: Scriabin, Op. 8 No. 12, bars 34–55; Scott Gorrie typesetting (2007), pp. 4–6. The return begins at A tempo; bars 52–55 contain the ascent and closing chords. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/f3/IMSLP273680-PMLP07375-Scriabin_Op.8_No_12.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A White House workshop
cues.text: On 4 November 2009 Awadagin Pratt plays this étude at a classical-music workshop and concert at the White House. Michelle Obama introduces Pratt, Joshua Bell, Alisa Weilerstein and Sharon Isbin as “the best in the world”. Pratt, she adds, began on a dusty upright his mother bought for a hundred dollars.
cues.evidence: Remarks by the First Lady at the Classical Music Series workshops, East Room, 2:22 p.m., 4 November 2009 (“They are the best in the world, and we’re incredibly lucky to have them today”; Pratt’s dusty upright piano “for just a hundred dollars”), with the video of the one-hour workshop and concert, White House page “White House Workshop: Classical Music” (the transcript carries the release date 26 October 2009). https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/photos-and-video/video/white-house-workshop-classical-music The Commons description of this recording places Pratt’s performance of the étude at about 29:40–31:44 of that video. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:20091104_Awadagin_Pratt_-_Scriabin,_%C3%89tude_Op._8_No._12.ogg

transitions.title: The melody softens; the bass keeps moving
transitions.from: A · Octaves above a leaping bass
transitions.how: Scriabin writes diminuendo, then piano, as the octave melody settles into a more winding phrase. The left hand keeps its triplets and its wide leaps; the bass carries on through the change of character.
transitions.evidence: Scriabin, Op. 8 No. 12, bars 16–19; Scott Gorrie typesetting (2007), p. 3. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/f3/IMSLP273680-PMLP07375-Scriabin_Op.8_No_12.pdf

transitions.title: Triplet chords fill both hands
transitions.to: A′ · Chords crowd around the melody
transitions.how: A crescendo and a brief ritardando prepare the return. At A tempo, the D♯ minor melody comes back above low bass octaves, but its accompaniment has spread into both hands. The right hand holds the tune while repeating chords underneath it.
transitions.evidence: Scriabin, Op. 8 No. 12, bars 32–36; Scott Gorrie typesetting (2007), p. 4. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/f3/IMSLP273680-PMLP07375-Scriabin_Op.8_No_12.pdf

transitions.title: Up the keyboard, then three chords
transitions.from: A′ · Chords crowd around the melody
transitions.to: Coda · A sweep and three chords
transitions.how: The two hands climb together through the keyboard. Their last high chord is cut short by a rest; two more chords answer lower down, the final one held for a whole bar. All three spell D♯ minor.
transitions.evidence: Scriabin, Op. 8 No. 12, bars 52–55; Scott Gorrie typesetting (2007), p. 6. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/f3/IMSLP273680-PMLP07375-Scriabin_Op.8_No_12.pdf

composer.epithet: He wrote a part for coloured light that had to be omitted at the work’s first performance.
facts: Moscow Conservatory, 1888–92: Safonov, Taneyev and Arensky
Piano professor at the Moscow Conservatory from 1898
Publisher Mitrofan Belyayev; conductor Serge Koussevitzky
Ten piano sonatas; three symphonies; a concerto; The Poem of Ecstasy and Prometheus
composer.background:
At the Moscow première of Prometheus in 1911, Scriabin sat at the piano and Serge Koussevitzky conducted. The audience heard the huge orchestra, the solo piano and the harmonies which seem to hang in the air before the first horn melody. One part of the score remained silent and invisible: the keyboard intended to project coloured light. Alexander Mozer had built a small apparatus for Scriabin, but Scriabin withdrew it from the concert because of technical difficulties. The lights were dropped. Scriabin had written for an instrument the concert hall could scarcely accommodate.

He was born in Moscow in 1872. His mother, Lyubov, was a trained pianist; she died when he was a baby. With his father pursuing a diplomatic career abroad, his aunt, also Lyubov, helped bring him up. He entered the cadet corps in 1882, took lessons from Nikolai Zverev, and joined Vasily Safonov’s piano class at the Moscow Conservatory in 1888. Rachmaninoff studied there too. Scriabin graduated as a pianist in 1892, a year after Rachmaninoff, but left without completing the composition course with Sergei Taneyev and Anton Arensky.
